Acceptance summary:

This manuscript uses light sheet microscopy, expression patterns of neurogenic genes, and lineage tracing experiments to study the development of the central nervous system in the octopus O. vulgaris. It will be of broad interest to scientists in the field of evolutionary developmental and neurobiology.

Decision letter after peer review:

Thank you for submitting your article "Identification of neural progenitor cells and their progeny reveals long distance migration in the developing octopus brain" for consideration by eLife. Your article has been reviewed by 3 peer reviewers, including Sonia Sen as the Reviewing Editor and Reviewer #1, and the evaluation has been overseen by Catherine Dulac as the Senior Editor. The following individual involved in review of your submission has agreed to reveal their identity: Shuichi Shigeno (Reviewer #2).

The reviewers have discussed their reviews with one another, and the Reviewing Editor has drafted this to help you prepare a revised submission.

We appreciated the quality, thoroughness and insights that this manuscripts provides. We had a few concerns that the authors could easily address, and these are listed below:

1) What is the nature of the migratory cells? The authors have shown that the migratory cells are largely elav+, post-mitotic cells. We're concerned that the low magnification images shown in the figures might miss that there are other cell types that migrate in the transition zones. Could the authors please provide higher magnification images of these regions and comment on whether they think other cell types – for example, glia or progenitors – might also be migrating from the LL to the cords?

2) Is the lateral lip the only neurogenic region? We noticed a low level of expression of ascl1 as well as PCNA in the developing brain cords. Is it possible that there's also a pool of progenitors in the brain cords? Once again, could the authors please provide higher magnification images of this and comment on it? If there are a pool of progenitors that do divide in the developing brain (albeit a smaller number) we suggest modifying the text accordingly.

Related to these essential points are comments in the individual reviews. Could the authors please refer to them while addressing these two main concerns?

Reviewer #1 (Recommendations for the authors):

The lineage tracing experiments are beautiful! I had trouble navigating them, though. I found myself going back and forth between figure 1 and 6 to orient myself. It's possible that this is because I am unfamiliar with the neuroanatomy. But maybe the authors could consider unpacking this section a bit? This could be done by splitting this figure. For example – deal with only the optic lobe at stage IX first, then at stage XII. Next deal with PVL/PV similarly?

I got the impression that there might be temporal pattering within the regions as well? For example, PVL neurons seem to be born only at the early time points. What are the authors' thoughts on this?

Do the authors think that the lateral lip is what also contributes to postembryonic neurogenesis?

Reviewer #2 (Recommendations for the authors):

1) Classic histological and embryological studies of cephalopod brains have identified a stream-like cell clusters from neurogenic territories surrounding eye regions to the brain, but these regions develop to jaxta-neuronal or neurosecretory tissues called the paravertical body, subpedunculate tissues, neurosecretory tissue of vena cava, and anterior chamber organs as described in Young JZ (1970). Actually, many cells of the subpedunculate tissue are largely embedded in the optic lobes, and cells of the paravertical body are attached to the vertical lobe, and seen in the subvertical and basal lobes. Vascular associated tissues are in the subesophageal mass. Topographically, this study's new terms are corresponding to those developing tissues: lateral lip: LL = sub-buccal tissue and anterior chamber organ, ATZ = paravertical body, and PTX = subpedunculate tissues.

The readers would be convinced that the ectodermal neurogenic regions certainly produced migratory cells for many brain lobes with a stepwise developmental manner as in Figure 6 and 7, but might not be convinced that there are no other cell types migrating from the lateral lip to the brain lobes. Confirming cell types of migratory cells would be essential to propose the main conclusion of this study.

Also, these eye region wrapping optic lobe produce the white body, hematopoietic organs that might be easily labeled with leaked dye and the labeled cells distribute to many brain lobes. The neurotracing (Figure 6) is a really good study and Figure 6I would be the important figure, showing migratory cells may be neurons in the vertical lobe, but the marked cells look big size and not sure these are neurons or endothelial cells of the vasculature. At least a few enlarged figures would be required to characterize the cell types.

2) During the late embryonic stages, the octopus brain continues to develop dramatically to large size, but the expression of neurogenic genes examined in this study disappears. The lateral lip is also very restricted to small areas and the migratory cells can not expect to contribute to major neurogenesis of the brain. One idea may be that weak NeuroD expression and Sox-B1 marked stem-like populations or novel genes are used. This point may be included in the discussion shortly.

In mammalian brain, the migratory cell stream is important for producing certain cell types, e.g. GABAergic neurons in the developing cortex from the ganglionic eminence, but it is not the main contributor to shape the cortex. The ventricular zones mainly produce various cell types as many readers know. The neurogenin and other genes keep being expressed there. However, the octopus developing brain looks very different on this point, indicating octopus neurogenesis still remains a mystery. This view would be helpful for future studies.

In addition to this, there are three points that may increase the impact and justification for this study.

1) In the introductory or late figures, the possible boundaries of LL, ATZ, and PTX could be clearly marked. This is because these are key areas for the main story.

2) I think, as a supplementary, the neurosecretory tissues associated with eye regions could be explained to avoid confusion about what tissues are tracing, although a sentence only for anterior chamber organ is seen in Materials and methods.

3) "The lateral lips harbor the neurogenic zone whereas the developing cords are postmitotic". I almost agree with this, but this statement is a hypothesis where there are neurogenic cells for brain cords. Elav in situ hybridization might not be able to detect a small population of neurogenic cells in the developing brain. In other sentences, the authors need to be careful about progenitor cells that may be in the overall area of the developing brains. Actually an anonymous has a result of BrdU pulse-labeled and positive cells that are distributed in many areas of developing octopus brains, although there is one publication that might show possibly false-positive cells in the vertical lobe. Therefore, neurogenesis for octopus lobes remains controversial and we need more convincing experiments and conclusions.

Reviewer #3 (Recommendations for the authors):

Based on anti PH3 and Ov-pcna expression, cell divisions, which might be correlated with neural progenitor formation/division, can be seen across the areas where the supra- and subesophageal ganglia form, and are thus not restricted to the lateral lips. This expression pattern is also acknowledged in the Results section: "While at Stages VII.2 and IX, transcripts were found in most embryonic tissues (mouth apparatus, retina, lateral lips and cords, in the latter at lower intensity), transcripts gradually disappeared in the optic, cerebral, palliovisceral and pedal cords from Stage XI onwards." The absence of cell divisions in later stages does not prove that the neuroepithelium from which the brain potentially develops is not neurogenic, i.e. that all progenitors arise from the lateral lips – they might simply have ceased dividing. Secondly, the expression of genes (SoxB, ASC, neurogenin) that are consistently expressed in neural progenitors across the animal kingdom, are expressed in all areas of the developing brain. Contrary to the description given in the Results section, both Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn seem to be expressed in the whole developing brain in stages XV, Ov-ascl1 also in stage XVII and later (Figure 4).

I agree with the authors that the lateral lips are neurogenic regions. The cell lineage tracing data also clearly show the migration of neural precursors into various brain areas (confirming the results by Koenig et al); however, it is also possible that neural progenitors do arise from other regions of the developing brain. This is my main concern – that the data do not convincingly show that the lateral lips are the only areas with neurogenic potential. Corresponding statements/discussions in the results and Discussion sections should be amended accordingly. Additional studies such as cell lineage tracing in the developing cords or laser dissections of the lateral lips would reveal the degree of involvement of the lateral lips in brain neurogenesis.

In this next part of the review, I have subdivided my comments according to the sections in the manuscript.

Abstract

"Our results indicate that progenitors are located outside the central brain cords in the lateral lips adjacent to the eyes, suggesting that newly formed neurons migrate into the cords."

The starting point of the study has to be clarified. It seems that this is not a novel finding (see Koenig et al., 2016)

Introduction

The introduction tries to give an overview of the mechanisms of neurogenesis across the animal kingdom. This is difficult to achieve in a short paragraph given the complexity and diversity of the neural developmental processes and leads to statements that are rather inconclusive, e.g. 'In general, neural progenitor cells are generated from ectodermal cells and divide symmetrically and asymmetrically to generate all neurons of the nervous system'. To improve the introduction, I suggest to limit the background information to lophotrochozoan/molluscan neurogenesis, explain their phylogenetic position and leave the topic of the diversity of neural developmental processes for the discussion.

The authors should also include here that cell lineage tracing in the squid Dorytheutis pealeii has revealed that cells surrounding the eye placode contribute to the anterior chamber organ, the supraesophagial mass, the buccal mass and the buccal ganglion (Koenig et al., 2016).

"Studying species from this group thus brings an opportunity to understand the genetic drivers of the development of organ systems that evolved convergently with vertebrates."

Inaccurate and too vague. Depends on which organ system you are considering and which characters can be traced back to the last common ancestor.

Results

Paragraph 1, lines 91-119 – Please clarify which of the findings are novel. Based on the citations, it seems that the authors are merely confirming previous descriptions of the developing octopus nervous system. If this is the case, the description should be moved into the introduction section. If, on the other hand, the re-examination has yielded new insights, these should be stated clearly.

"Staining intensity increased by Stage XI, showing low-level staining in the lateral lips surrounding the eye placode and more intense staining in all cords and surrounding the mouth. A similar pattern was observed at subsequent stages with highest staining intensity in the central brain cords/masses and low intensity staining in the lateral lips"

Has the staining been quantified? Or is the intensity estimated? Could the difference in intensity be due to the cellular arrangement within the tissue, i.e. areas where more cells accumulate stain more strongly?

"In the central brain, (neuroD) transcripts were present at low level in the optic lobes, supra- and subesophageal masses. A similar expression pattern was visible at Stages XIX.1 and XX.2 with low level expression in all brain masses and clear presence in the transition zones."

The level of expression in the developing brain is the same as for ASC and neurogenin in Stage XV.2 and ASC in Stage XVII but the authors describe the expression of these two genes as absent. (e.g. "At subsequent stages of organogenesis (XI, XIII, XV.2 and XVII), Ov-ascl1 was expressed in the lateral lips and was absent from the developing cords/brain lobes.") This is an important point in the argumentation. Please clarify.

The data on the mitotic activity of subpopulations of neural progenitors expressing asc and neurogenin, respectively, are not convincing. The yellow anti-PH3 staining is so bright that it is not possible to see if it overlaps with the magenta/green of asc/neurogenin. In addition, the statement "Furthermore, co-staining with the PH3 antibody demonstrated that Ov-ascl1+ progenitor cells seem more proliferative compared to Ov-ngn+ progenitors, that rarely overlap with the PH3" needs additional support. First of all, Ovascl1+ progenitors might only divide once but there are simply more of them in the lateral lip. Secondly, the authors would have to analyse different time points since the Ov-ascl1+ and the Ov-nngn+ populations might be mitotically active at different times.

The corresponding sentence in the Discussion section "In O. vulgaris, the Ov ascl1 progenitor population seems to be more proliferative compared to the Ov-ngn progenitor population, which suggests their sequential expression could be turned around in cephalopods" should be amended accordingly.

"Occasionally, we identified few, single randomly dispersed cells in the pedal or palliovisceral lobes originating from more ventrally located progenitor populations. Considering the very low number of cells compared to the major output from those progenitors, these cells were not taken into account as they might have been labeled while migrating through another area."

If this is the case, the labelling technique needs to be explained better. If progenitors are labeled in a certain area of the lateral lip and their progeny then traced, how can cells then randomly pick up the dye?

Discussion

"This study showed that grossly, the embryonic octopus brain does not contain dividing progenitor

cells.

This is not what the data show and contradicts the statement in the Results section “While at Stages VII.2 and IX, transcripts were found in most embryonic tissues (mouth apparatus, retina, lateral lips and cords, in the latter at lower intensity), transcripts gradually disappeared in the optic, cerebral, palliovisceral and pedal cords from Stage XI onwards."

We further delineated embryonic neurogenesis in O. vulgaris using neural progenitor, pan-neuronal and differentiated-neuron marker genes with conserved functions in neurogenesis, neural specification and differentiation in protostomes and deuterostomes.

Inaccurate. 'Function' should be replaced by 'expression'. Different functions in neurogenesis have been reported for neural genes in different phyla/species and even within the same organism.

The authors also discuss a delay in neural maturation compared to other cephalopods based on the temporal expression of postmitotic neuronal markers; however, without explaining how embryonic stages can be compared between species, specifically in relation to other developmental processes, the discussion is not convincing.

Figures

Figures should be mentioned and sorted in the correct order, including figure panels. Please also consistently include the figure panel you are referring to.

Figure 1

In the transverse sections, the line indicating the subesophageal mass points to a cell-free area. Please correct.

What is the orientation of the reconstruction in panel E? The different lobes are not mentioned in the main text relating to figure 1. Please amend.

claims.source: Organogenesis starts at Stage VII.2 and can be split in early, mid-, and late phases (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Stated in text and shown in Figure 1A

claims.claim: In the early organogenesis phase, the brain anlagen (cordal) are elongated and interconnected (in three dimensions).
claims.source: In the early organogenesis phase, the brain anlagen (cordal) are elongated and interconnected (in three dimensions) (Figure 1A,B) as also described by Shigeno et al. for Octopus bimaculoides (Shigeno et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 1A,B and citation to Shigeno et al., 2015

claims.claim: The cerebral cord (CC) will give rise to the lobes of the supraesophageal mass (SEM).
claims.source: On the most anterior side, lateral and posterior to the mouth and foregut, the cerebral cord (CC) will give rise to the lobes of the supraesophageal mass (SEM), while on the posterior side of the embryo, the palliovisceral (PVC) and pedal (PC) cords will form the subesophageal mass (SUB).
claims.evidence: Based on developmental observations and anatomical knowledge

claims.claim: The palliovisceral (PVC) and pedal (PC) cords will form the subesophageal mass (SUB).
claims.source: On the most anterior side, lateral and posterior to the mouth and foregut, the cerebral cord (CC) will give rise to the lobes of the supraesophageal mass (SEM), while on the posterior side of the embryo, the palliovisceral (PVC) and pedal (PC) cords will form the subesophageal mass (SUB).
claims.evidence: Based on developmental observations and anatomical knowledge

claims.claim: The two bilateral optic cords (OC) will differentiate and grow to form the optic lobes (OL).
claims.source: The two bilateral optic cords (OC) will differentiate and grow to form the optic lobes (OL) (Figure 1A,C).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 1A,C showing developmental progression

claims.claim: At hatching, the central brain surrounds the esophagus and contains densely packed nuclei.
claims.source: At hatching, the central brain that now surrounds the esophagus is considerably big and contains densely packed nuclei (Figure 1D).
claims.evidence: Supported by Figure 1D showing DAPI staining

claims.claim: The tissue adjacent to the eye primordia first grows in size from Stage VII.2 to Stage XV.2, and then shrinks to disappear at hatching.
claims.source: In contrast to the growing brain cords, the tissue adjacent to the eye primordia first grows in size from Stage VII.2 to Stage XV.2, and then shrinks to disappear at hatching, suggesting this tissue might contribute to the inner head structures (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Observed in developmental series shown in Figure 1A

claims.claim: The tissue adjacent to the eye primordia might contribute to the inner head structures.
claims.source: In contrast to the growing brain cords, the tissue adjacent to the eye primordia first grows in size from Stage VII.2 to Stage XV.2, and then shrinks to disappear at hatching, suggesting this tissue might contribute to the inner head structures (Figure 1A).
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on the tissue's growth and disappearance pattern

claims.claim: The tissue adjacent to the eye primordia was first described as 'Kopflappen' by Marquis.
claims.source: This tissue was first described as 'Kopflappen' by Marquis and later as 'anterior chamber organ' by Koenig et al., 2016; Marquis, 1989; Shigeno et al., 2001; Yamamoto et al., 2003.
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Marquis, 1989

claims.claim: The term 'anterior chamber organ' was introduced by Young, referring to neurovenous tissue adjacent to the adult eye.
claims.source: However, the term 'anterior chamber organ' was introduced by Young, referring to neurovenous tissue adjacent to the adult eye, that presumably regulates the fluid content between the lens and cornea (Young, 1970).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Young, 1970

claims.claim: The structure adjacent to the eye is not restricted to the anterior side of each eye, but is rather placed lateral to the eye fields.
claims.source: The term was most likely wrongly adopted embryonically as the tissue at that stage is not restricted to the anterior side of each eye, but is rather placed lateral to the eye fields.
claims.evidence: Based on 3D imaging observations

claims.claim: Based on 3D light sheet imaging, the structure adjacent to the eye is connected to the central brain through a stream-like transition zone.
claims.source: Based on 3D light sheet imaging, we could clearly show that the structure is also connected to the central brain, through a stream-like transition zone.
claims.evidence: Based on light sheet microscopy data

claims.claim: The tissue adjacent to the eye was renamed to 'lateral lips' based on its position and shape.
claims.source: Because of its position and shape, we renamed the tissue to 'lateral lips' (LL, indicated in mint green in Figure 1C,E) and introduced the terms 'anterior transition zone' (ATZ) and 'posterior transition zone' (PTZ) for the region that interconnects the lateral lips with the central brain on the anterior or posterior side of the embryo, respectively (Figure 1C,F).
claims.evidence: Authors' nomenclature decision based on anatomical observations shown in Figure 1C,E,F

claims.claim: Three candidate elav transcripts were identified in O. vulgaris.
claims.source: Through blast searches against the full-length transcriptome of O. vulgaris embryos and paralarval brains generated in this study (see Materials and methods), we identified three candidate elav transcripts.
claims.evidence: Based on transcriptome analysis performed in this study

claims.claim: One of the O. vulgaris ELAV candidate proteins nested with vertebrate HuC/D and invertebrate neural ELAV homologs.
claims.source: One of the O. vulgaris ELAV candidate proteins nested with vertebrate HuC/D and invertebrate neural ELAV homologs. We refer to this sequence as Ov-ELAV.
claims.evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: The two other ELAV candidate proteins could be identified as non-neural.
claims.source: The two other candidate proteins could be identified as non-neural (Figure 2—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: An ELAV/HuD family splicing factor domain was detected in Ov-ELAV, which is characteristic of ELAV proteins.
claims.source: We also performed a conserved domain (CD)-Search and detected an ELAV/HuD family splicing factor domain which is characteristic of ELAV proteins.
claims.evidence: Based on conserved domain search analysis

claims.claim: Ov-elav transcripts were detected throughout development with little expression at Stage IX in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal, and optic cords.
claims.source: Ov-elav transcripts were detected throughout development with little expression at Stage IX in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal, and optic cords (Figure 2A).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2A

claims.claim: Strong Ov-elav staining was observed from Stage XI onwards, with low-level staining in the lateral lips and more intense staining in all cords and surrounding the mouth.
claims.source: Strong staining was observed from Stage XI onwards, with low-level staining in the lateral lips surrounding the eye placode and more intense staining in all cords and surrounding the mouth (Figure 2B).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2B

claims.claim: At Stage XIII, a region in between the lateral lips and the central brain on the posterior side of the embryo showed intermediate Ov-elav expression, corresponding to the posterior transition zone (PTZ).
claims.source: At Stage XIII, a region in between the lateral lips and the central brain on the posterior side of the embryo showed intermediate Ov-elav expression. This region corresponds to the posterior transition zone (PTZ), introduced earlier (Figure 2C).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2C

claims.claim: From Stage XV.2 onwards, cells on the anterior side of the embryo and laterally from the supraesophageal mass, corresponding to the anterior transition zone (ATZ), showed intermediate Ov-elav expression levels.
claims.source: From Stage XV.2 onwards, cells on the anterior side of the embryo and laterally from the supraesophageal mass, corresponding to the anterior transition zone (ATZ), showed intermediate Ov-elav expression levels as well (Figure 2D,E).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2D,E

claims.claim: In the optic lobes at stages XIX.1 and XX.2, Ov-elav expression was highest in the medulla and inner granular layer, but lower in the outer granular layer.
claims.source: In the optic lobes at stages XIX.1 and XX.2, Ov-elav expression was highest in the medulla and inner granular layer, but lower in the outer granular layer.
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization observations

claims.claim: The ATZ and PTZ shrink toward the end of embryonic development and seem to become integrated in the developing brain.
claims.source: The ATZ and PTZ shrink toward the end of embryonic development and seem to become integrated in the developing brain (Figure 2F,G).
claims.evidence: Based on observations shown in Figure 2F,G

claims.claim: Neuronal differentiation is present at early organogenesis phases in O. vulgaris.
claims.source: In summary, our data indicate that neuronal differentiation is present at early organogenesis phases already, and the transition zones as well as the growing cords and masses contain large numbers of differentiating neurons.
claims.evidence: Inference based on Ov-elav expression data

claims.claim: The transition zones as well as the growing cords and masses contain large numbers of differentiating neurons.
claims.source: In summary, our data indicate that neuronal differentiation is present at early organogenesis phases already, and the transition zones as well as the growing cords and masses contain large numbers of differentiating neurons.
claims.evidence: Inference based on Ov-elav expression data

claims.claim: Ov-syt was first detected in the retina at Stage XI.
claims.source: In O. vulgaris, we observed expression of Ov-syt in the retina from Stage XI onwards (Figure 2H,I).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2H,I

claims.claim: Ov-syt was first expressed in the outer layers of the optic cord at Stage XIII.
claims.source: In the central brain, it was first expressed in the outer layers of the optic cord at Stage XIII, and in the optic lobe medulla, supra- and subesophageal masses from Stage XV.2 onwards, pointing to a sequential maturation (Figure 2J–N).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2J-N

claims.claim: Ov-syt was expressed in the optic lobe medulla, supra- and subesophageal masses from Stage XV.2 onwards, pointing to a sequential maturation.
claims.source: In the central brain, it was first expressed in the outer layers of the optic cord at Stage XIII, and in the optic lobe medulla, supra- and subesophageal masses from Stage XV.2 onwards, pointing to a sequential maturation (Figure 2J–N).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 2J-N; inference about sequential maturation

claims.claim: First low-level immunoreactivity against acetylated alpha tubulin was found from Stage XV.2 onwards within the optic lobes.
claims.source: First low-level immunoreactivity against acetylated alpha tubulin was found from Stage XV.2 onwards within the optic lobes (Figure 2O–U).
claims.evidence: Based on immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 2O-U

claims.claim: The embryonic cords demonstrate clear signs of differentiation from Stage XV.2 onwards.
claims.source: We therefore used the adult terminology (optic lobe, supra- and subesophageal mass) for CNS annotation from this stage onwards, since the embryonic cords demonstrate clear signs of differentiation.
claims.evidence: Inference based on Ov-syt expression and acetylated alpha-tubulin immunoreactivity

claims.claim: PCNA is a nuclear protein required for DNA replication and repair, and functions as a cofactor of DNA polymerase-delta in eukaryotes and archaea.
claims.source: PCNA is a nuclear protein required for DNA replication and repair, and functions as a cofactor of DNA polymerase-delta in eukaryotes and archaea (Barry and Bell, 2006; Baserga, 1991; Prelich et al., 1987).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Barry and Bell, 2006; Baserga, 1991; Prelich et al., 1987

claims.claim: Expression of pcna is tightly regulated and peaks at late G1 and S phases of the cell cycle.
claims.source: Expression of pcna is tightly regulated and peaks at late G1 and S phases of the cell cycle (Santos et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Santos et al., 2015

claims.claim: Ov-pcna transcripts were detected throughout embryonic development.
claims.source: Ov-pcna transcripts were detected throughout embryonic development (Figure 3A–D,I–L).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A-D,I-L

claims.claim: At Stages VII.2 and IX, Ov-pcna transcripts were found in most embryonic tissues (mouth apparatus, retina, lateral lips and cords, in the latter at lower intensity).
claims.source: While at Stages VII.2 and IX, transcripts were found in most embryonic tissues (mouth apparatus, retina, lateral lips and cords, in the latter at lower intensity), transcripts gradually disappeared in the optic, cerebral, palliovisceral and pedal cords from Stage XI onwards (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A-C

claims.claim: Ov-pcna transcripts gradually disappeared in the optic, cerebral, palliovisceral and pedal cords from Stage XI onwards.
claims.source: While at Stages VII.2 and IX, transcripts were found in most embryonic tissues (mouth apparatus, retina, lateral lips and cords, in the latter at lower intensity), transcripts gradually disappeared in the optic, cerebral, palliovisceral and pedal cords from Stage XI onwards (Figure 3A–C).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3A-C

claims.claim: At Stage XI, most Ov-pcna expressing cells that were found adjacent to the eye, located to an area that is Ov-elav negative and that might be part of the epithelium lining the sinus ophthalmicus.
claims.source: At Stage XI, most Ov-pcna expressing cells that were found adjacent to the eye, located to an area that is Ov-elav negative and that might be part of the epithelium lining the sinus ophthalmicus (Figure 3C).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3C; speculation about tissue identity

claims.claim: Ov-pcna transcripts were dispersed throughout the lateral lips and were absent from the transition zones and central brain at Stages XIII-XX.2.
claims.source: Ov-pcna transcripts were dispersed throughout the lateral lips and were absent from the transition zones and central brain at Stages XIII-XX.2 (Figure 3D,I–L).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 3D,I-L

claims.claim: Histone H3 is phosphorylated on serine 10 and serine 28 during early mitosis and dephosphorylated at the end of mitosis in eukaryotes.
claims.source: Histone H3 is phosphorylated on serine 10 and serine 28 during early mitosis and dephosphorylated at the end of mitosis in eukaryotes (Hans and Dimitrov, 2001; Prigent and Dimitrov, 2003; Wei et al., 1998).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Hans and Dimitrov, 2001; Prigent and Dimitrov, 2003; Wei et al., 1998

claims.claim: Mitotic activity in the embryonic head region was high at the beginning of organogenesis, with the highest level of dividing cells present in the mouth apparatus, at the apical side in the developing retina and spread throughout the lateral lips.
claims.source: Immunohistochemistry on embryonic tissue from Stage VII.2 to XX.2 showed that mitotic activity in the embryonic head region was high at the beginning of organogenesis, with the highest level of dividing cells present in the mouth apparatus, at the apical side in the developing retina and spread throughout the lateral lips (Figure 3E–H,M–P).
claims.evidence: Based on PH3 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3E-H,M-P

claims.claim: The number of PH3-positive cells in the cerebral, optic, palliovisceral and pedal cords was limited, with possibly very few, single, dim and seemingly randomly organized positive cells present until Stage XIII.
claims.source: Consistent with Ov-pcna expression, the number of PH3-positive cells in the cerebral, optic, palliovisceral and pedal cords was limited, with possibly very few, single, dim and seemingly randomly organized positive cells present until Stage XIII (Figure 3E–H).
claims.evidence: Based on PH3 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3E-H

claims.claim: At late organogenesis and maturation stages, PH3-positive cells located to the lateral lips and were absent from the central brain.
claims.source: At late organogenesis and maturation stages, PH3-positive cells located to the lateral lips and were absent from the central brain (Figure 3M–P).
claims.evidence: Based on PH3 immunohistochemistry shown in Figure 3M-P

claims.claim: The lateral lips represent a major octopus neurogenic zone.
claims.source: Given that the elav-positive areas are almost devoid of dividing cells, and the transition zone represents an area connecting the mitotically active lateral lips to the growing CNS, our data strongly suggest that the lateral lips represent a major octopus neurogenic zone.
claims.evidence: Inference based on Ov-elav, Ov-pcna, and PH3 expression patterns

claims.claim: O. vulgaris has single homologs for SOXC, D and E and two SOXB homologs.
claims.source: Based on phylogenetic analysis including 31 SOXB, 3 SOXC, 4 SOXD, 4 SOXE, and 3 SOXF amino acid sequences from other species together with 5 TCF/LEF sequences to root the tree, we identified single O. vulgaris homologs for SOXC, D and E and two SOXB homologs (Figure 4—figure supplement 1).
claims.evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: One O. vulgaris SOXB protein nested within the SOXB2 clade and the other one within the SOXB1 clade.
claims.source: One O. vulgaris SOXB protein nested within the SOXB2 clade and the other one within the SOXB1 clade, the latter named Ov-SOXB1.
claims.evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: CD-Search of Ov-SOXB1 protein revealed the highly conserved SOX-TCF HMG-box and SOXp superfamily domains.
claims.source: CD-Search of this Ov-SOXB1 protein revealed the highly conserved SOX-TCF HMG-box and SOXp superfamily domains.
claims.evidence: Based on conserved domain search analysis

claims.claim: Ov-soxB1 transcript levels were high in the head region at all embryonic stages examined.
claims.source: Ov-soxB1 transcript levels were high in the head region at all embryonic stages examined (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2

claims.claim: At Stage IX, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the lateral lips, eyes and surface ectoderm surrounding the mouth apparatus.
claims.source: At Stage IX, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the lateral lips, eyes and surface ectoderm surrounding the mouth apparatus (esophagus, radula, salivary gland).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization observations

claims.claim: At Stage IX, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the cerebral cord, but not in the palliovisceral, pedal and optic cords.
claims.source: In the developing central brain, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the cerebral cord, but not in the palliovisceral, pedal and optic cords (Figure 4—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2A-D

claims.claim: At Stage XI, Ov-soxB1 was highly expressed in the lateral lips and cerebral cord, and transcripts were present in the optic cord in a patched pattern.

claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2E-H

claims.claim: At Stage XIII, Ov-soxB1 transcripts were most highly expressed in the cerebral cord and showed a similar patched pattern in the optic cords, and were present in the pedal cord and limited in the palliovisceral cord.
claims.source: At Stage XIII, Ov-soxB1 transcripts were most highly expressed in the cerebral cord and showed a similar patched pattern in the optic cords. Transcripts were also present in the pedal cord and limited in the palliovisceral cord (Figure 4—figure supplement 2I–L).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2I-L

claims.claim: At Stage XV.2, Ov-soxB1 expression was high in the lateral lips and supraesophageal mass, spread in the subesophageal mass, and highest in the inner granular layer of the optic lobes.
claims.source: At Stage XV.2, Ov-soxB1 expression was high in the lateral lips and supraesophageal mass. In the subesophageal mass, Ov-soxB1-positive cells were more spread and in the optic lobes, Ov-soxB1 transcripts showed the highest expression in the inner granular layer, while expression was more distributed in the outer granular layer and medulla (Figure 4—figure supplement 2M–P).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2M-P

claims.claim: At Stages XIX.1 and XX.2, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the lateral lips, the supra- and subesophageal mass and optic lobes where it was most highly expressed in the inner granular layer.
claims.source: At Stages XIX.1 and XX.2, Ov-soxB1 was expressed in the lateral lips, the supra- and subesophageal mass and optic lobes where it was most highly expressed in the inner granular layer (Figure 4—figure supplement 2U-b).
claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 2U-b

claims.claim: Ov-soxB1 was not only expressed in putative stem cells, but also in postmitotic (Ov-elav+) areas.
claims.source: Taken together, Ov-soxB1 was not only expressed in putative stem cells, but also in postmitotic (Ov-elav+) areas, as has been described for other invertebrate species.
claims.evidence: Inference based on Ov-soxB1 and Ov-elav expression patterns; comparison to other species

claims.claim: Phylogenetic analysis effectively assigned Ov-neuroD and Ov-ngn to their respective subfamilies.
claims.source: Phylogenetic analysis of the atonal-related bHLH transcription factors including 15 NEUROD and 8 NEUROGENIN/TAP protein sequences from other species effectively assigned Ov-neuroD and Ov-ngn to their respective subfamilies (Figure 4—figure supplement 3).
claims.evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 3

claims.claim: CD-Search identified conserved bHLH domains in Ov-neuroD and Ov-ngn.

claims.evidence: Based on conserved domain search analysis; supported by citations to Jones, 2004; Murre et al., 1989

claims.claim: Phylogenetic analysis placed Ov-ASCL1 within the proneuronal ASCa subgroup of the bHLH superfamily.

claims.evidence: Based on phylogenetic analysis shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 4

claims.claim: CD-Search revealed a highly conserved DNA-binding bHLH domain in Ov-ASCL1.
claims.source: CD-Search revealed a highly conserved DNA-binding bHLH domain.
claims.evidence: Based on conserved domain search analysis

claims.claim: At Stage IX, Ov-ascl1 was expressed in the lateral lips surrounding the eye primordia, in retinal cells of the developing eyes and in the tissue delineating the mouth apparatus, and was absent from the cerebral, pedal, palliovisceral and optic cords.

claims.claim: At subsequent stages of organogenesis (XI, XIII, XV.2, and XVII), Ov-ascl1 was expressed in the lateral lips and was absent from the developing cords/brain lobes.

claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4B-E

claims.claim: During maturation and right before hatching, the number of cells expressing Ov-ascl1 significantly decreased with the thinning lateral lips and transcripts were still absent from the optic lobes, supra- and subesophageal masses.

claims.claim: Ov-ngn transcripts were found in the lateral lips throughout organogenesis and maturation phases, while transcripts were absent from the developing brain cords.

claims.claim: Very few Ov-ngn transcripts were present in both transition zones at Stages XIII to XX.2.

claims.evidence: Based on in situ hybridization shown in Figure 4M,N

claims.claim: Expression of both Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn consistently marks the proliferative lateral lips, with Ov-ascl1 expressing cells being more numerous compared to Ov-ngn expressing cells.
claims.source: In summary, expression of both Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn consistently marks the proliferative lateral lips, with Ov-ascl1 expressing cells being more numerous compared to Ov-ngn expressing cells.
claims.evidence: Summary inference based on Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn expression patterns

claims.claim: At the beginning of organogenesis (Stage IX and XI), Ov-neuroD was expressed in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal and optic cords of the central nervous system.

claims.claim: At Stages XV.2 and XVII, high level Ov-neuroD expression marked both the anterior and posterior transition zones.

claims.claim: The proximity of Ov-ngn+ cells to dividing Ov-ascl1+ progenitors could be a sign of asymmetric progenitor division during neurogenesis in octopus.
claims.source: The proximity of Ov-ngn+ cells to dividing Ov-ascl1+ progenitors could be a sign of asymmetric progenitor division during neurogenesis in octopus.
claims.evidence: Speculative inference based on spatial relationship of cell types

claims.claim: Ov-neuroD expressing cells did not co-localize with PH3 immunoreactive cells, indicating that Ov-neuroD is absent from mitotically active cells in octopus embryos, at least at Stage XV.2.

claims.claim: If the progenitor cells in the lateral lips would contribute neurons to the CNS, postmitotic neurons would need to travel long distances from the lateral lips to the central brain.

claims.claim: At hatching, the major lobes described for the adult supra- and subesophageal masses can be distinguished.
claims.source: At hatching, the major lobes described for the adult supra- and subesophageal masses can be distinguished, with the supraesophageal mass consisting of buccal, inferior frontal, superior frontal, subfrontal, vertical, subvertical, basal, dorsal basal and medial basal lobes, and the subesophageal mass consisting of the palliovisceral and pedal lobes (Figure 6A–C; Young, 1971).
claims.evidence: Based on anatomical observations shown in Figure 6A-C; supported by citation to Young, 1971

claims.claim: Progenitor cells in the lateral lips generate output to the different lobes in the supra- and subesophageal masses.
claims.source: For these regions, we identified progenitor cells in the lateral lips that generate output to the different lobes in the supra- and subesophageal masses (Figure 6D–J).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 6D-J

claims.claim: A major contribution to the palliovisceral lobe found its origin in progenitor cells in the dorsal-posterior quadrant of the lateral lips at Stage IX.
claims.source: Specifically, a major contribution to the palliovisceral lobe found its origin in progenitor cells in the dorsal-posterior quadrant of the lateral lips at Stage IX, as was suggested but not empirically proven by Koenig et al., 2016 (example in Figure 6D–E).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6D-E; supported by citation to Koenig et al., 2016

claims.claim: Progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lip distinctly contributed cells to the inferior and superior frontal lobes of the supraesophageal mass at all stages.
claims.source: In addition, progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lip distinctly contributed cells to the inferior and superior frontal lobes of the supraesophageal mass at all stages, which has not been reported before by Koenig et al., 2016 (example in Figure 6G–H).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6G-H; comparison to Koenig et al., 2016

claims.claim: Progenitor cells in the ventral lateral lips produced cells destined to the basal lobes (basal lobe, dorsal basal lobe, medial basal lobe) of the supraesophageal mass.
claims.source: Progenitor cells in the ventral lateral lips also produced cells destined to the basal lobes (basal lobe, dorsal basal lobe, medial basal lobe) of the supraesophageal mass (orange and red injection spots in Figure 6D,G,I).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6D,G,I

claims.claim: The majority of cells located in the supraesophageal mass were derived from ventral-anterior progenitor cells in the lateral lips.
claims.source: The majority of cells located in the supraesophageal mass, however, were derived from ventral-anterior progenitor cells in the lateral lips (example in Figure 6D,F,I,J).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6D,F,I,J

claims.claim: Few labeled progenitor populations generated cells for the pedal lobe of the subesophageal mass.
claims.source: In contrast to the supraesophageal mass and the palliovisceral lobe, few labeled progenitor populations generated cells for the pedal lobe of the subesophageal mass.
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing observations

claims.claim: Ventral-anterior progenitor populations at Stage XV.2 generated cells for the pedal lobe.
claims.source: Apart from the ventral-anterior progenitor populations at Stage XV.2 (example in Figure 6I–J), we did not identify progenitor populations that gave rise to a significant number of cells that migrated to the pedal lobe.
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 6I-J

claims.claim: Progenitor cells in the dorsal-anterior quadrant of the lateral lips gave rise to cells in the optic lobes, for which labeled cells generally located to the inner and outer granular layers of the cortex.
claims.source: Focusing on the output to the optic lobe and peduncle complex (Figure 7), we identified progenitor cells in the dorsal-anterior quadrant of the lateral lips that gave rise to cells in the optic lobes, for which labeled cells generally located to the inner and outer granular layers of the cortex (black populations with an asterisk in Figure 7A,C,E; example of progeny in Figure 7D).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 7A,C,E,D

claims.claim: Progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lips at Stages IX and XII.1 generated optic lobe cells that resided in the medulla.
claims.source: Progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lips at Stages IX and XII.1 generated optic lobe cells that resided in the medulla, while at Stage XV.2, more cells located to the optic lobe cortex as well (example in Figure 7A,B,E,F).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 7A,B,E,F

claims.claim: At Stage XV.2, progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lips generated more cells that located to the optic lobe cortex.
claims.source: Progenitor cells in the posterior lateral lips at Stages IX and XII.1 generated optic lobe cells that resided in the medulla, while at Stage XV.2, more cells located to the optic lobe cortex as well (example in Figure 7A,B,E,F).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 7A,B,E,F

claims.claim: Ventral-anterior lateral lip progenitors did not generate optic lobe cells.
claims.source: Ventral-anterior lateral lip progenitors did not generate optic lobe cells.
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing observations

claims.claim: Progenitors in the posterior and ventral lateral lips generated cells destined to the peduncle complex (olfactory and peduncle lobe).
claims.source: We also identified a clear spatial patterning of progenitors that generate cells for the peduncle complex (olfactory and peduncle lobe). Progenitors in the posterior and ventral lateral lips generated cells destined to this complex (example in Figure 7A–B), while populations on the dorsal-anterior side did not.
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing shown in Figure 7A-B

claims.claim: Populations on the dorsal-anterior side of the lateral lips did not generate cells for the peduncle complex.
claims.source: We also identified a clear spatial patterning of progenitors that generate cells for the peduncle complex (olfactory and peduncle lobe). Progenitors in the posterior and ventral lateral lips generated cells destined to this complex (example in Figure 7A–B), while populations on the dorsal-anterior side did not.
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing observations

claims.claim: The lineage tracing study identified spatial and temporal patterning in the lateral lips, which generate neurons for specific brain regions.
claims.source: Taken together, our lineage tracing study identified spatial and temporal patterning in the lateral lips, which generate neurons for specific brain regions.
claims.evidence: Summary inference based on lineage tracing experiments

claims.claim: Labeled cells in the lateral lips divided and migrated posteriorly and entered the posterior transition zone.
claims.source: Labeled cells in the lateral lips (intense labeling, Figure 8G–L) divided and migrated posteriorly and entered the posterior transition zone (labeling intensity decreased, Figure 8D–F).

claims.claim: Cells could be traced towards the ventral side of the embryo in the posterior transition zone after which they occupied all layers in the optic lobe.
claims.source: Then, cells could be traced towards the ventral side of the embryo in the posterior transition zone (Figure 8F–P) after which they occupied all layers in the optic lobe (Figure 8G–R).
claims.evidence: Based on short-term lineage tracing shown in Figure 8F-R

claims.claim: Forty-eight hr tracing combined with HCR showed migrating cells in the posterior transition zone that expressed Ov-neuroD and low-level Ov-elav, indicative of newly formed neurons.
claims.source: Forty-eight hr tracing combined with HCR on thin sections showed migrating cells in the posterior transition zone that expressed Ov-neuroD and low-level Ov-elav, indicative of newly formed neurons (Figure 8—figure supplement 2A–D).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing combined with HCR shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2A-D

claims.claim: The first cells that reached the optic lobe expressed Ov-elav, confirming their neuronal identity.
claims.source: The first cells that reached the optic lobe expressed Ov-elav, confirming their neuronal identity (Figure 8—figure supplement 2B,E).
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing combined with HCR shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 2B,E

claims.claim: Populations labeled at different locations in the lateral lips showed similar trajectories, with cells passing the dorsal and posterior lateral lips before entering the posterior transition zone and then the optic lobe.
claims.source: Populations labeled at a different location in the lateral lips showed similar trajectories (even the most anterior labeled population in Figure 8—figure supplement 1), with cells passing the dorsal and posterior lateral lips before entering the posterior transition zone and then the optic lobe.
claims.evidence: Based on multiple lineage tracing experiments shown in Figure 8—figure supplement 1

claims.claim: Cells destined for the optic lobe seem to take a defined path via the posterior transition zone.
claims.source: Taken together, cells destined for the optic lobe seem to take a defined path via the posterior transition zone.
claims.evidence: Summary inference based on trajectory mapping experiments

claims.claim: The embryonic octopus brain is practically devoid of dividing cells from Stage XI onwards.
claims.source: This study showed that the embryonic octopus brain is practically devoid of dividing cells from Stage XI onwards.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from Ov-pcna and PH3 data

claims.claim: A transient embryonic structure surrounding the developing eye – the lateral lips – harbors proliferative cells expressing conserved pro-neural transcription factors.
claims.source: Instead, we identified a transient embryonic structure surrounding the developing eye – the lateral lips – that harbors proliferative cells expressing conserved pro-neural transcription factors.
claims.evidence: Summary of findings from Ov-pcna, PH3, Ov-ascl1, and Ov-ngn data

claims.claim: The spatiotemporal expression patterns of neurogenic genes suggest their involvement in regulating the development of the CNS in O. vulgaris.
claims.source: The spatiotemporal expression patterns of these neurogenic genes suggest their involvement in regulating the development of the CNS in O. vulgaris.
claims.evidence: Inference based on expression patterns of multiple neurogenic genes

claims.claim: Koenig et al. have suggested a basic fate map of the neural primordia in D. pealeii using DiI tracing experiments, and identified contributions of cells from the lateral lips to the developing central brain.
claims.source: Koenig et al. have suggested a basic fate map of the neural primordia in D. pealeii using DiI tracing experiments, and identified contributions of cells from the lateral lips to the developing central brain (Koenig et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Koenig et al., 2016

claims.claim: The spatial map of progenitor contributions seems to be conserved in cephalopods.

claims.evidence: Inference based on comparison of lineage tracing results in O. vulgaris with D. pealeii

claims.claim: Patterning in the lateral lips is established at early neurogenesis stages and is grossly temporally maintained, suggesting that lobe-specificity is determined early on within the progenitor area.
claims.source: In addition, we show that patterning is established at early neurogenesis stages and is grossly temporally maintained, suggesting that lobe-specificity is determined early on within the progenitor area.
claims.evidence: Inference based on lineage tracing at different developmental stages

claims.claim: Long-distance migration of cells generated in the lateral lips towards the central brain occurs in octopuses.
claims.source: Next to clear spatial patterning in the lateral lips, we identified long-distance migration of cells generated in the lateral lips towards the central brain in octopuses.
claims.evidence: Based on lineage tracing and trajectory mapping experiments

claims.claim: In O. bimaculoides, Ov-elav expression was already reported from Stage VII.2 onwards, pointing toward rapid neuronal differentiation.
claims.source: In O. bimaculoides, expression was already reported from Stage VII.2 onwards, pointing toward rapid neuronal differentiation (Shigeno et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Shigeno et al., 2015

claims.claim: In S. officinalis, Sof-elav1 expression is unequally distributed over the different cords, and disappears toward the end of embryonic development, pointing to a different timing of neuronal differentiation and a more advanced maturation of the Sepia brain at hatching.
claims.source: In contrast to both octopus species, Sof-elav1 expression in the cuttlefish Sepia officinalis is unequally distributed over the different cords, and disappears toward the end of embryonic development, pointing to a different timing of neuronal differentiation and a more advanced maturation of the Sepia brain at hatching (Buresi et al., 2013).
claims.evidence: Supported by citation to Buresi et al., 2013; inference about maturation timing

claims.claim: S. officinalis embryos have been described to respond to tactile and chemical as well as visual cues from within the egg capsule from Stage XV.1 and XVI onwards, respectively.
claims.source: Consistent with this, S. officinalis embryos have been described to respond to tactile and chemical as well as visual cues from within the egg capsule from Stage XV.1 and XVI onwards, respectively (Romagny et al., 2012) (for interspecies stage comparison, see Deryckere et al., 2020).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Romagny et al., 2012 and Deryckere et al., 2020

claims.claim: O. vulgaris embryos only seem to react to visual stimuli (chromatophore contraction in response to light change) and mechanical stimuli (mantle contraction after tapping the chorion) from Stage XIX.1 onwards.
claims.source: In our hands, O. vulgaris embryos only seem to react to visual stimuli (chromatophore contraction in response to light change) and mechanical stimuli (mantle contraction after tapping the chorion) from Stage XIX.1 onwards (preliminary observation).
claims.evidence: Based on preliminary observations by the authors

claims.claim: Neural processes visualized with immunostaining against acetylated alpha-tubulin revealed the presence of neurites in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal, and optic cords of O. bimaculoides and S. officinalis embryos as early as Stage VIII.
claims.source: Furthermore, neural processes visualized with immunostaining against acetylated alpha-tubulin revealed the presence of neurites in the cerebral, palliovisceral, pedal, and optic cords of O. bimaculoides and S. officinalis embryos as early as Stage VIII, while we only observed expression of Ov-syt and presence of acetylated alpha-tubulin in the central brain from Stages XIII and XV.2 onwards, respectively (Baratte and Bonnaud, 2009; Shigeno et al., 2015).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Baratte and Bonnaud, 2009; Shigeno et al., 2015

claims.claim: These findings support the delayed maturation of the brain in O. vulgaris, that perhaps uses its paralarval phase to complete maturation of the nervous system.
claims.source: These findings further support the delayed maturation of the brain in O. vulgaris, that perhaps uses its paralarval phase to complete maturation of the nervous system.
claims.evidence: Inference based on comparative developmental timing; speculation about paralarval maturation

claims.claim: Ov-soxB1 expression is not restricted to neurectodermal progenitor regions.

claims.claim: Consistent with Sof-soxB1 expression in S. officinalis, Ov-soxB1 is expressed at high level in the surface ectoderm, in the developing eyes, and is absent from the gills and stellate ganglia.

claims.evidence: Based on Ov-soxB1 expression observations; supported by citation to Focareta and Cole, 2016

claims.claim: soxB1 is expressed in sensory epithelia in vertebrates, invertebrate mollusks and acoelomate worms.
claims.source: Next to (neur)ectodermal expression, soxB1 is also expressed in sensory epithelia in vertebrates, invertebrate mollusks and acoelomate worms (Focareta and Cole, 2016; Guo et al., 2010; Kiernan et al., 2005; Le Gouar et al., 2004; Neves et al., 2007; Semmler et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by multiple citations

claims.claim: SOXB1 proteins are present in both neurectodermal stem cells and differentiated neurons in certain species.
claims.source: In addition, SOXB1 proteins are present in both neurectodermal stem cells and differentiated neurons in certain species.
claims.evidence: Draws from established knowledge about SOXB1 function

claims.claim: Drosophila soxN and Schmidtea polychroa soxB1 are expressed in early specification events in the CNS, but also in differentiated parts where they are involved in neuronal differentiation and axonal patterning, suggesting a dual role for protostome soxB1.
claims.source: Drosophila soxN and Schmidtea polychroa soxB1 for example are expressed in early specification events in the CNS, but also in differentiated parts where they are involved in neuronal differentiation and axonal patterning, suggesting a dual role for protostome soxB1 (Ferrero et al., 2014; Girard et al., 2006; Monjo and Romero, 2015; Phochanukul and Russell, 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Ferrero et al., 2014; Girard et al., 2006; Monjo and Romero, 2015; Phochanukul and Russell, 2010

claims.claim: Some subtypes of (inter)neurons require SOXB1 proteins for proper specification and migration in vertebrates.
claims.source: While such a general function in neuronal differentiation of vertebrate soxB1 factors has not been shown, some subtypes of (inter)neurons do require SOXB1 proteins for proper specification and migration (Cavallaro et al., 2008; Ekonomou et al., 2005; Panayi et al., 2010).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Cavallaro et al., 2008; Ekonomou et al., 2005; Panayi et al., 2010

claims.claim: Expression data suggest a dual role for Ov-soxB1, in early nervous system development to specify neural fate, and later on to steer neural cell differentiation.
claims.source: Similar to many other species, our expression data suggest a dual role for Ov-soxB1, in early nervous system development to specify neural fate, and later on to steer neural cell differentiation.
claims.evidence: Inference based on Ov-soxB1 expression pattern; comparison to other species

claims.claim: The expression pattern of Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn suggests the presence of a neurogenic domain in the lateral lips, outside the cords of the central brain.

claims.evidence: Inference based on Ov-ascl1 and Ov-ngn expression patterns shown in Figure 9A,B

claims.claim: In the annelids Capitella teleta and P. dumerilii, neurogenin and ash1 are both expressed in actively proliferating neural progenitor cells in the neurectoderm.
claims.source: In the annelids Capitella teleta and P. dumerilii, neurogenin and ash1 are both expressed in actively proliferating neural progenitor cells in the neurectoderm (Figure 9C).
claims.evidence: Draws from established knowledge; shown in Figure 9C

claims.claim: In C. teleta, Ct-ngn positive cells stay on the apical side, while Ct-ash1-positive progenitors ingress and undergo limited division before becoming Ct-elav positive.

claims.claim: In O. vulgaris, the Ov-ascl1 progenitor population seems to be more proliferative compared to the Ov-ngn progenitor population, at least at Stage XV.2 (late organogenesis), which suggests their sequential expression could be turned around in cephalopods.
claims.source: In O. vulgaris, the Ov-ascl1 progenitor population seems to be more proliferative compared to the Ov-ngn progenitor population, at least at Stage XV.2 (late organogenesis), which suggests their sequential expression could be turned around in cephalopods (Figure 9B,C).
claims.evidence: Based on HCR data shown in Figure 9B,C; inference about sequential expression

claims.claim: The Ov-elav expressing neurons in the cords are not located immediately basal from the Ov-ascl1 or Ov-ngn positive pool of neural progenitor cells.

claims.claim: A population of Ov-neuroD expressing cells is found in the transition zones, in between the Ov-ascl1+ and Ov-ngn+ lateral lips and the developing Ov-elav+ brain, suggesting an intermediate, Ov-neuroD+ population is present in O. vulgaris.

claims.claim: neuroD genes can be widely found in bilaterians, where they steer the differentiation of neurons.

claims.claim: In vertebrates, ascl1 and ngn are expressed in a complementary fashion, both exerting proneuronal functions in neurogenesis.

claims.claim: Drosophila has only one neurogenin/neuroD homolog called tap, which relates better to neurogenin based on sequence similarities, but does not have a proneural role and is expressed in a few neurons, regulating their differentiation, axonal growth and guidance.
claims.source: In contrast, Drosophila has only one neurogenin/neuroD homolog called tap, which relates better to neurogenin based on sequence similarities, but does not have a proneural role and is expressed in a few neurons, regulating their differentiation, axonal growth and guidance (Gautier et al., 1997; Vervoort and Ledent, 2001; Yuan et al., 2016).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Gautier et al., 1997; Vervoort and Ledent, 2001; Yuan et al., 2016

claims.claim: In arthropods, the members of the achaete-scute subfamily are expressed in proneural clusters and promote the generation of neural progenitor cells from quiescent ectodermal cells.
claims.source: In arthropods, the members of the achaete-scute subfamily are expressed in proneural clusters and promote the generation of neural progenitor cells from quiescent ectodermal cells (Bertrand et al., 2002; Cubas et al., 1991; Quan and Hassan, 2005; Skeath and Carroll, 1991; Stollewerk and Chipman, 2006).
claims.evidence: Supported by citations to Bertrand et al., 2002; Cubas et al., 1991; Quan and Hassan, 2005; Skeath and Carroll, 1991; Stollewerk and Chipman, 2006

claims.source: In O. bimaculoides, neurogenin and neuroD transcripts were detected in the prospective cerebral, palliovisceral and pedal cords at Stage VIII, based on whole mount in situ hybridization, but did not distinguish the lateral lips from the cordal areas (Shigeno et al., 2015).

claims.claim: The lateral lips harbor proliferating cells with a signature of neural progenitors, while mature neurons are found in the cords.
